author: original (NevaIB)
title: The nuclear atom
themeLabel: Models of the particulate nature of matter
islUnits: 1. Atomic theory and kinetic theory (Y12 Sep)
bigPicture: An atom is a tiny, dense, positive nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons. The number of protons fixes the element; changing the number of neutrons gives isotopes, which behave the same chemically but differ in mass. Relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of those isotope masses.

keyIdeas.cue: What is inside an atom and how do you read a nuclear symbol?
keyIdeas.answer: Nucleus: protons (relative mass 1, charge +1) and neutrons (mass 1, charge 0); electrons (mass ≈ 1/1840, charge −1) occupy the space outside. In the symbol with mass number A above and atomic number Z below: protons = Z, neutrons = A − Z, electrons = Z − (ion charge). Actual masses and charges are in the data booklet; the electron's mass can be treated as negligible.

keyIdeas.cue: What are isotopes and how is a non-integer Ar calculated?
keyIdeas.answer: Atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A). Same chemical properties (same electron arrangement) but different physical properties such as density, rate of diffusion and, for radioactive isotopes, stability. Ar = Σ(isotope mass × fractional abundance), which is why Ar is usually not a whole number.

keyIdeas.cue: How is a mass spectrum used to find Ar?
keyIdeas.answer: Each peak is an isotope: its position on the x-axis is the mass/charge ratio (m/z, effectively the isotope mass for 1+ ions) and its height is the relative abundance. Multiply each m/z by its abundance, add, and divide by the total abundance. How the spectrometer works is not assessed.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you find isotope abundances from Ar?
keyIdeas.answer: For two isotopes, let one abundance be x % and the other (100 − x) %. Then Ar = [m₁x + m₂(100 − x)] / 100; solve for x. Check: Ar must lie between the two isotope masses and nearer the more abundant one.

keyTerms.def: A proton or neutron (particle in the nucleus).
Number of protons; defines the element.
Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
Weighted mean mass of an element's atoms relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom; no units.
Mass-to-charge ratio plotted on the x-axis of a mass spectrum.

misconceptions.wrong: Isotopes of an element react differently.
misconceptions.right: Chemistry depends on electrons; isotopes have the same electron configuration, so they react the same way. Only physical properties differ.

misconceptions.wrong: Mass number is the same as relative atomic mass.
misconceptions.right: Mass number is a whole number for one isotope; Ar is a weighted average over all isotopes.

misconceptions.wrong: A 2− ion has two fewer electrons.
misconceptions.right: Negative charge means electrons gained: a 2− ion has two more electrons than protons.

misconceptions.wrong: Ar is the mass of the most common isotope.
misconceptions.right: It is the weighted mean of all isotopes, so it is usually not a whole number.
